title: This time is different?
summary: Sarah Breeden, Deputy Governor for Financial Stability at the Bank of England, delivered a speech on April 17, 2026 assessing whether the financial system has learned from past crises and identifying current vulnerabilities. She acknowledges the system has proved resilient through six major shocks since 2020, but warns that risks have migrated from banks to market-based finance, private markets, and sovereign balance sheets. Breeden highlights three key structural vulnerabilities: the rapid growth of private markets to ~$18 trillion in global AuM, elevated sovereign debt near post-war highs, and complexity in interconnected financial ecosystems.
key_points: Global financial system absorbed six major shocks since 2020 (pandemic, Ukraine war, bank failures including a G-SIB, UK gilt crisis, trade disruptions, energy shock) without systemic amplification
UK bank stress tests show the banking system can continue lending through severe but plausible scenarios, reflecting significantly improved capital and liquidity buffers post-GFC
Market-based finance now accounts for ~50% of UK and global financial-sector assets, shifting risk from bank deposits to investors better placed to absorb losses
Global private-market assets under management rose ~6x since 2008/9 to approximately $18 trillion by 2025, with limited transparency, lagging valuations, and layer-cake leverage
Public debt in advanced economies is near post-war highs, reducing fiscal space and increasing sensitivity to shifts in market confidence; UK gilt market experienced severe stress in autumn 2022
Three salient vulnerabilities: private credit markets, sovereign balance sheets, and complex financial ecosystem connections that can propagate stress rapidly
Recent credit concerns include weakening investor sentiment, weakened underwriting standards, and series of defaults (MFS, Tricolor, First Brands Group) with redemption pressures emerging
why_it_matters: This speech provides the BoE's official assessment of current financial stability risks and structural vulnerabilities, directly relevant for market participants, policymakers, and risk managers. The shift of risk from well-regulated banks to less-transparent private markets and sovereigns represents a fundamental change in market structure that could amplify future shocks. Understanding where stress could propagate—in repo and derivatives markets anchored by sovereign bonds—is critical for positioning and risk management.
macro_context: While the speech focuses on financial stability rather than monetary policy, it notes that rising government bond yields tighten financing conditions across the economy and that reduced fiscal space limits governments' ability to respond to future shocks—both with macro implications for growth and policy flexibility.
market_structure_context: The speech directly addresses market structure: the migration of activity from banks to market-based finance (~50% of assets), the growth of private markets ($18 trillion AuM), sovereign bond markets as core plumbing for repo and derivatives, and complex ecosystem connections between banks, insurers, reinsurers, and private credit that make losses harder to trace.
important_numbers: ~50% (share of UK/global financial-sector assets in market-based finance)
